content: 1. During pregnancy or labor, the presence of illicit substances such as cocaine can be detected through positive urine tests in either the mother or the infant. This is a critical marker for identifying substance use during pregnancy. 2. Specialist midwives with expertise in drug treatment services provide comprehensive care, including modeling parent-child interactions, monitoring infant health, and offering parent education and skills training. Tools such as the Hawaii Early Learning Profile and the Carolina Preschool Curriculum are utilized to support developmental outcomes. 3. At 36 months, child behavior is assessed using the Child Behavior Checklist, as demonstrated in studies like Dakof 2003 in the USA, which involved 103 postpartum participants with positive cocaine urine tests. 4. Interventions often include 20-minute to 1-hour sessions, conducted 1 to 4 times per week over 8 weeks, led by specialist midwives experienced in drug dependence treatment. These sessions may involve individual, family, or case management approaches. 5. Treatment programs aim to improve retention rates, with evaluations at 4 weeks and 90 days, as seen in studies like Quinlivan 2000 in Australia, which included 136 participants identified at their first antenatal appointment with a history of alcohol or illicit drug use. 6. Nurse midwives provide a range of services, including lactation and mothercraft education, general and obstetric health surveillance, contraception and child health advice, and parenting skills education. They also ensure vaccination appointments are confirmed and provide information on drug and alcohol services. 7. Weekly home visits from birth to 6 months, transitioning to biweekly visits until 18 months, are conducted by lay African American women in some programs. These visits aim to empower mothers, enhance their problem-solving abilities, and improve mother-infant interactions, as observed using tools like the Child Abuse Potential Inventory and the Bayley Scales of Infant Development. 8. The Seattle Birth to 3 Years Program links families to care, offers parenting classes, therapeutic childcare, and substance abuse treatment programs. It employs para-professional advocates with similar life experiences to the participants, providing weekly visits for 6 weeks, then bi-monthly visits for 3 years. 9. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) such as Black 1994, Bartu 2006, and Dakof 2003 have been assessed for risks of bias. While some trials had low selection bias, all were at high risk for performance bias due to the inability to blind interventions. Attrition bias was also significant in some studies, with high loss-to-follow-up rates. 10. Heterogeneity in studies is evident, with variations in home visitor type, visit frequency, duration, and content. Subgroup analyses attempt to address these differences, but inconsistencies and uncertainties remain, leading to downgrading of evidence quality. 11. Motivational interviewing during pregnancy and postpartum has been explored in trials, involving three individual sessions based on motivational techniques. Clinicians receive specialized training, and participants are offered additional sessions as part of treatment-as-usual programs. 12. Comprehensive federal demonstration projects provide free services for women using illicit substances during pregnancy. These include motivational interviewing sessions and educational controls, such as videos on substance use and supplementary home visits. 13. Maternal outcomes in these interventions include treatment utilization, frequency of attendance at therapy sessions, and urine screens negative for all drugs. Infant outcomes are not always applicable in these studies. 14. Quality assessments of included RCTs highlight risks of bias, including selection, performance, detection, attrition, and reporting biases. These factors influence the reliability of findings and the interpretation of outcomes. 15. Meta-analyses of RCTs reveal heterogeneity in results, with moderate to high variability in intervention types, visit frequency, and content. Random effects models are often used to account for this variability, but the analyses are frequently downgraded for inconsistency. 16. Guidelines for the identification and management of substance use and substance use disorders in pregnancy emphasize the importance of tailored interventions, including home visits, motivational interviewing, and comprehensive care programs, to address the unique needs of this population.
